issues.legal_issue: A Supreme Court decision declares law under Article 141 when it independently decides a legal issue directly before it, even if a party has conceded a related point.
material_facts: The constitutional validity of the 1971 amendments was directly in issue in the earlier appeals.
Although a respondent had consented to the High Court judgments being set aside, the Supreme Court independently held the amendments constitutionally valid.
The Supreme Court also stated that interim payments ended upon the Director’s original determination.
issues.conclusion: The earlier Supreme Court decision declared law binding under Article 141: it upheld the amendments and determined the period for which interim payments were payable.
issues.legal_principle: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts. The ratio is the principle reached from the judgment as a whole in light of the issues before the Court, not an isolated sentence or factual finding. A point disposed of only on concession does not declare law, but the Court’s independent decision of an issue directly before it does. The Court applied the principles discussed in Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Shri Sri Krishna Sinha, Krishena Kumar v. Union of India, State of U.P. v. Synthetics and Chemicals Ltd., Arnit Das v. State of Bihar, A-One Granites v. State of U.P., Kulwant Kaur v. Gurdial Singh Mann, and Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Gurnam Kaur.

predicates.constitutional_validity_directly_contest: The constitutional validity of an amendment was directly in issue in the earlier proceeding.
predicates.court_independently_examined_amendment: The court considered the amendment independently rather than relying only on a party’s concession.
predicates.appeal_concerns_binding_effect_of_suprem: The proceeding concerns whether an earlier Supreme Court decision binds the parties or courts.

issues.definition: When constitutional validity was directly contested and independently examined in an earlier decision, a proceeding about that decision’s binding effect treats the determination as binding law.

issues.legal_issue: An earlier unappealed judgment does not preserve an enforceable direction when its sole legal basis is later displaced by a binding Supreme Court decision.
material_facts: The respondents obtained mandamus based on a High Court decision that held the amendments invalid.
The State did not appeal the mandamus granted to the respondents, and it became final between them.
The Supreme Court later reversed the High Court decision and held the amendments constitutionally valid.
The respondents sought to enforce their earlier direction after that Supreme Court decision.
issues.conclusion: The earlier mandamus did not give the respondents an indefeasible right enforceable after the Supreme Court decision displaced the legal basis for it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 141, a Supreme Court declaration of law binds everyone, including persons whose similar High Court judgments were not appealed. In M/s Shenoy & Co. v. Commercial Tax Officer, the Court held that a mandamus based on a law declared invalid by a High Court becomes ineffective when the Supreme Court holds that law valid. The Court distinguished the finality and res judicata principles discussed in Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Smt. Deorajin Debi, State of West Bengal v. Hemant Kumar Bhattacharjee, and Authorised Officer (Land Reforms) v. M.M. Krishnamurthy Chetty, and applied Shenoy.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_enforcement_of_unappeal: A party seeks to enforce a judgment that the opposing party did not appeal.
predicates.earlier_direction_depended_solely_on_rev: The earlier direction rested solely on a legal conclusion later displaced by a higher court.
predicates.supreme_court_declared_different_binding: The Supreme Court later declared a legal rule that conflicts with the basis of the earlier direction.

issues.definition: An unappealed direction based solely on a legal conclusion later displaced by binding Supreme Court law is not enforceable on that former basis.

issues.legal_issue: A writ of mandamus requires a subsisting legally enforceable right and cannot compel performance contrary to binding law.
material_facts: The respondents sought a fresh mandamus requiring the State to make interim payments under the Act.
Their claimed right depended on the amendments being constitutionally invalid and interim payments continuing beyond the Director’s determination.
The Supreme Court had upheld the amendments and declared that interim payments ended upon the Director’s original determination.
The claimed right therefore did not subsist when the later mandamus was sought.
issues.conclusion: The High Court could not issue mandamus because the respondents had no subsisting legally enforceable right to the payments they claimed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 226 empowers High Courts to issue writs, including mandamus, for fundamental rights and other legal purposes, subject to recognised limits. Mandamus requires a subsisting legal right in the applicant and a corresponding legal duty in the respondent public authority. The Court relied on Kalyan Singh v. State of U.P. for the requirement that the right subsist on the date of the petition.

predicates.proceeding_seeks_mandamus: A party seeks a judicial command requiring a public authority to act.
predicates.claimed_right_no_longer_subsists: The legal right relied on by the applicant had ceased to be enforceable by the time the writ was sought.
predicates.public_authority_is_asked_to_perform_cor: The requested command would require a public authority to perform a duty said to correspond to the claimed right.

issues.definition: When mandamus is sought for a public authority’s performance of a duty but the applicant’s claimed right no longer subsists, mandamus cannot issue.

issues.legal_issue: A precedent addressing the binding effect of Supreme Court decisions need not be reconsidered merely because it did not discuss res judicata.
material_facts: The State relied on the rule in Shenoy concerning the effect of Supreme Court law on unappealed judgments.
The respondents argued that Shenoy should be reconsidered because it had not addressed res judicata and related principles.
The Court concluded that Shenoy addressed the binding effect of Supreme Court law in cases where appeals had not been filed and that the asserted omission did not justify reconsideration.
issues.conclusion: The Court declined to refer Shenoy for reconsideration and reaffirmed its conclusion.
issues.legal_principle: Article 141 requires uniform application of the law declared by the Supreme Court. The Court followed the three-judge decision in M/s Shenoy & Co. v. Commercial Tax Officer and held that its non-consideration of res judicata was not a reason to reconsider it.

predicates.proceeding_requests_reconsideration_of_p: A party asks the court to reconsider an existing precedent.
predicates.precedent_addresses_binding_effect_of_su: The precedent considered how Supreme Court law applies where related judgments were not appealed.
predicates.objection_is_only_nonconsideration_of_re: The asserted ground for reconsideration is that the precedent did not address res judicata.

issues.definition: A precedent on the binding effect of Supreme Court law in unappealed cases does not require reconsideration when the sole objection is its omission of res judicata.
